title: Social Change through Financial Innovation: Evidence from Donor-Advised Funds
venue_or_publisher: Review of Corporate Finance Studies 11(3):694-735 (SSRN version 2021, doi:10.2139/ssrn.3925198)
method: New economic-purpose classification of DAFs; conditional correlations
data_and_period: 'New data' on DAF sponsors (sponsor-level); period not stated in abstract
main_finding: Growth is fastest among DAFs offering fintech tools, liquidity transformation of complex assets and DEI-focused grantmaking; DAFs with an innovative service style grant more to high-inequality areas, in times of greatest need and to more efficient charities
comparison_note: Supports the repo's view that product and technology style, not legal sponsor type, separates sponsors. The repo's 3-type split (national/CF/single-issue) is the same one Grennan argues is insufficient. Correlational only

title: Community Diversity and Donor Control: An Empirical Analysis of Contributions to Donor-Advised Funds at Community Foundations
method: Regression of community-foundation contributions on local ethnic-racial diversity
data_and_period: Community foundation financial data (Form 990-based); years not stated in abstract
main_finding: Greater ethnic-racial diversity is associated with higher contributions to DAFs at community foundations but not with general (unrestricted) contributions
comparison_note: No overlap with repo figures. Adds a demand-side explanation for why donor-controlled vehicles grow inside CFs

authors: Phillips, Susan D.; Dalziel, Katherine; Sjogren, Keith
title: Donor Advised Funds in Canada, Australia and the US: Differing Regulatory Regimes, Differing Streams of Policy Drift
method: Comparative regulatory analysis with three donor-motivation scenarios (pseudo-foundation, tax saving, privacy)
data_and_period: Regulatory regimes and aggregate DAF statistics, three countries, to c.2020
main_finding: Regulation shapes DAF use; Australia's regime is less skewed to tax-motivated donors so DAF assets are proportionately lower; questions whether DAFs democratise philanthropy; all three countries show policy drift
comparison_note: Consistent with the repo's international comparison; no figure conflicts

authors: Heist, H. Daniel; Farwell, Megan M.; Cummings, Benjamin F.; Cnaan, Ram A.; Andrews, Erinn; Shamash, Rebecca
title: Understanding the Donor-Advised Fund Giving Process: Insights From Current DAF Users
method: 48 in-depth qualitative interviews with DAF users
main_finding: DAF giving follows a four-phase process with multiple decision points and wide individual adaptation
comparison_note: Qualitative donor-journey evidence; complements the repo's complaint corpus

authors: Heist, H. Daniel; Cummings, Benjamin F.; Farwell, Megan M.; Cnaan, Ram; Andrews, Erinn
title: Tubs, tanks, and towers: Donor strategies for donor-advised funds giving
method: Same 48 interviews; typology
main_finding: Three strategies: tubs (flow-through annually), tanks (lump sum granted out in the near term), towers (sustained long-term giving)
comparison_note: Gives a behavioural reason why aggregate payout (23.7-28.4%) and account medians (about 9-11%) diverge

authors: Biagi, James B.; Hefter, Mark L.
title: Donor advised funds: Ethical issues on the new frontier of philanthropy
method: Legal and ethical analysis
main_finding: Sets out legal and ethical principles for sponsoring, receiving from and contributing to DAFs and the main legal and ethical risks for charities
comparison_note: Practitioner-legal framing; no empirical overlap

title: Donor-Advised Funds and Impact Investing: A Practitioner's View (2024 reissue with prologue: doi:10.9707/1944-5660.1695)
peer_review_status: practitioner article in a reviewed journal
method: Practitioner essay
main_finding: Sponsors face particular barriers to impact investing: they must persuade boards and investment committees and lack foundation-style program staff
comparison_note: Fits the repo's finding that pool choice is as large a cost lever as sponsor choice (§11.4); no figures

title: Show Me the Money: Addressing the Oversight Gap in Private Foundation Donations to Donor-Advised Funds
retrieval_evidence: Repository record page with abstract (DOI resolves there), 2026-11-15
method: Doctrinal analysis plus policy design
data_and_period: Cites 2018 DAF assets of at least $72bn
main_finding: Private-foundation grants to DAFs count toward the 5% payout but carry no time limit and obscure recipients; proposes a two-part federal and state fix
comparison_note: The repo nets DAF-to-DAF transfers but does not measure foundation-to-DAF inflows. The CA AG audit (L29) puts them at $1.1-1.7bn a year at 57 sponsors

title: Speeding Up Benefits to Charity by Reforming Gifts to Intermediaries
method: Legal-policy analysis of the ACE Act
data_and_period: Cites $1.26tn held in DAFs and private foundations
main_finding: Gifts to intermediaries delay public benefit while the tax benefit is immediate; the ACE Act is sound but should also cover existing DAF accounts; asks whether DAFs at mission-driven sponsors (e.g. CFs) deserve different treatment
comparison_note: Agrees with §6 that the ACE Act is not enacted and that no DAF payout rule exists; adds the 'existing accounts' design point
independence_note: Author is a long-standing advocate of DAF payout reform

authors: Brakman Reiser, Dana; Dean, Steven A.
title: For-Profit Philanthropy: Elite Power and the Threat of Limited Liability Companies, Donor-Advised Funds, and Strategic Corporate Giving (ch. 3 'Commercially Affiliated Donor-Advised Fund Sponsors', doi:10.1093/oso/9780190074500.003.0003)
retrieval_evidence: Crossref records + abstracts for book and chapter, 2026-11-15
method: Legal-historical analysis ('Grand Bargain' of 1969: timing, targeting, transparency)
main_finding: Commercially affiliated sponsors now dominate the field (four of the ten largest US charity recipients) and escape the 1969 timing, targeting and transparency rules
comparison_note: Matches the repo's finding that about 39% of assets sit at three affiliate-linked nationals. The repo adds that sponsor assets are unconcentrated (HHI about 830), which the book does not address

title: Donor Advised Funds & Delay: An Intergenerational Justice Solution?
method: Normative and comparative legal analysis (US, UK, Canada, Australia, NZ)
main_finding: Proposes procedural duties on sponsor decision-makers to weigh intergenerational justice when deciding how much to spend or retain, as an alternative to a fixed payout rate
comparison_note: A policy option the repo's regulatory tracker does not list

title: Donor-Advised Funds in the Wake of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act
venue_or_publisher: Columbia Journal of Tax Law 14(1):1-29 (SSRN 2022, doi:10.2139/ssrn.4227391)
retrieval_evidence: Crossref record + abstract; DOI resolves to the journal page (HTTP 302 checked), 2026-11-15
method: Descriptive evidence plus tax-policy analysis
main_finding: Bunching to clear the TCJA standard deduction likely drives much of the rise in new DAF accounts since 2016; for bunchers, asset accumulation is not the main problem, the fiscal cost relative to incremental giving is; payout rules do not address it
comparison_note: The repo shows reported account counts are dominated by donation processors (79.5% of FY2024 accounts) and that FY2022 account growth flips from +72% to -7% without Givinga. On a strict advisory-privilege basis accounts still rose from 1.12m (FY2021) to 2.59m (FY2024). Walker's premise of rapid account growth survives on the strict count, but evidence based on headline NPT counts needs the corrected series. OBBBA's 0.5%-of-AGI floor from 2026 strengthens his bunching mechanism

authors: Vance-McMullen, Danielle; Heist, H. Daniel (DAF Research Collaborative)
title: Donor-Advised Fund Account Patterns and Trends (2017-2020)
venue_or_publisher: DAF Research Collaborative report (executive summary PDF created 2022-03-21)
method: Descriptive analysis of account-level records
data_and_period: 13,000 accounts at 21 community foundations and religious sponsors, 2017-2020; excludes national sponsors
main_finding: Median four-year average account payout is 11% (13% for spendable DAFs); 35% of accounts pay out under 5% and 13% pay out 50% or more; 10% are formally endowed (18% of $1m+ accounts)
comparison_note: Gives the account-level distribution the repo says is not public, for CF and religious sponsors only. The 11% account median is close to the repo's CF sponsor median (about 11%), but it measures a different thing. Secondary sources sometimes attribute these percentages to the 2024 National Study

title: Self-Regulating Donor Advised Funds: An Analysis of Inactive Account Policies and Endowed DAFs
venue_or_publisher: DAF Research Collaborative / BYU working paper, 6 January 2023
method: Content analysis of written sponsor policies
data_and_period: Policies of the 150 largest US DAF sponsors (c.2022)
main_finding: 83-91% of sponsors (over 88% of sampled assets) have written inactive-account policies; on average they intervene after 36 months without grants and allow 18 months to respond before closing the account or taking over grantmaking; 47% offer endowed DAFs, more often at smaller sponsors
comparison_note: The repo's incentive table rates retention incentives as documented but their effect on payout as unsupported. Policy existence is not enforcement: the 2025 manager survey (L23) finds only 35% put great emphasis on active grantmaking
independence_note: Funded by Philanthropy Roundtable (an opponent of DAF payout mandates)

authors: Heist, H. Daniel; Vance-McMullen, Danielle; Kienker, Brittany; Williams, Jeff (DAF Research Collaborative)
title: The National Study on Donor Advised Funds
venue_or_publisher: DAF Research Collaborative / Dorothy A. Johnson Center for Philanthropy
retrieval_evidence: Executive summary PDF downloaded and read; Crossref records for 10.4087/ymfd7624 and 10.4087/xoai8853, 2026-11-15
method: Descriptive analysis of pooled, anonymised account-level records; three-year average payout
data_and_period: Over 50,000 accounts at 111 voluntary DAF programs (nationals, CFs, religious), over 600,000 contributions and 2.25m grants, 2014-2022
main_finding: Median three-year account payout is 9% (15% excluding inactive accounts) and the mean is 18%; 22% of accounts made no grants in 2020-22 (45% of these opened in 2020 or later); 49% hold under $50k; Q4 brings 57% of contributions but only 32% of grants; under 4% of grants are anonymous; 58% of accounts had granted out 100% of the original contribution after eight years
comparison_note: The repo's aggregate payout of 23.7-28.4% (19.0-21.5% net of DAF-to-DAF transfers) is consistent with an account median of 9%: a few large, fast-paying accounts carry the aggregate. This is the best account-level evidence available, but it is a voluntary sample whose national-sponsor coverage is not disclosed in the summary. §1 should cite it rather than say fund-level payout is simply not public

title: Reshaping Charity Channels: How Assets Flow into and out of Donor-Advised Funds
venue_or_publisher: SSRN working paper 2024; published 2025 in Springer Series in Supply Chain Management, pp.47-71 (doi:10.1007/978-3-031-74994-0_4)
retrieval_evidence: Crossref records + abstract for both DOIs, 2026-11-15 (SSRN page itself returned a bot challenge)
method: Comparison of DAF sponsors with other public charities on asset types received and recipient sectors
main_finding: DAFs take in disproportionately more noncash gifts, especially those with extra tax incentives; DAF funds often cycle between sponsors; DAF grants go disproportionately to education and religion at the expense of human services and health
comparison_note: Agrees on sponsor-to-sponsor cycling (repo: 11.2% of top-50 FY2023 Schedule I dollars; 12.1% of nationals' grants to other nationals). The repo's top-50 FY2023 shares are education 27.0%, religion 13.1%, human services 13.5%, health 11.7%. The religion tilt is a national-sponsor feature (14.1% vs 2.9% at CFs). The repo has no 'other giving' benchmark, so the 'at the expense of' comparison is new
independence_note: Flannery is research director of the IPS Charity Reform Initiative, a DAF-reform advocate

title: Are Donor-Advised Funds Facilitating Opaque Giving to Politically Engaged Charities?
method: Recipient-level comparison of DAF sponsor grants with other giving sources; private-foundation revenue share as an opacity proxy
data_and_period: Form 990 / Schedule I grants (years per paper)
main_finding: DAF sponsors grant to politically engaged charities at about 1.7 times the rate of other sources, and to anti-government and hate groups at about 3.5 times; DAFs supply over a quarter of those groups' contributions; the tilt rises with the share of sponsor revenue that comes from private foundations
comparison_note: The repo does not cover recipient politics. This is a regulatory-pressure risk relevant to the §4966/§6033 guidance project and to sponsor grant review (§4)

title: Charitable Objectives or Donor Benefits? What Sponsor Language Reveals About Donor-Advised Fund Priorities and Resource Allocation
venue_or_publisher: Nonprofit and Voluntary Sector Quarterly 55(1):57-89 (SSRN 2023, doi:10.2139/ssrn.4565216)
method: Text measure of sponsor website language (charitable objectives vs donor benefits) linked to Form 990 outcomes
data_and_period: Sponsor websites and Form 990 data (years per paper)
main_finding: National sponsors stress donor benefits more and vary most within type; among nationals, more emphasis on donor benefits strongly predicts larger DAF assets, mainly through lower payout rather than higher contributions
repo_sections: §3 (incentive table: asset-based fee alignment, effect on payout unsupported [RT])
comparison_note: The first peer-reviewed sponsor-level evidence linking a commercial orientation to lower payout. It is correlational and measures marketing language, not fee structure. It could move the §3 row from 'unsupported' to 'suggestive' if a validator accepts language as a proxy for retention orientation

title: Community Leadership and Donor-Advised Funds: Navigating Logics of Donor Services and Community Leadership in Community Foundations
method: Exploratory mixed methods (annual-report text plus Form 990)
main_finding: CFs with a stronger donor-service logic (a higher share of DAF-funded grants) show a broader range of community-leadership activities; the two logics coexist and may reinforce each other
comparison_note: Counters the 'DAFs crowd out CF mission' narrative at CF level. No overlap with repo figures

title: Getting Donor-Advised Funds Regulation Right: Closing the Public Support Test Loophole
venue_or_publisher: NYU Journal of Legislation and Public Policy 28:125 (SSRN doi:10.2139/ssrn.5147592)
method: Doctrinal and policy analysis, including the November 2023 proposed §4966 regulations
data_and_period: Doctrinal; cites a payout range of 9.7% (IPS) to 23.9% (NPT) for 2023
main_finding: The PPA 2006 extra-strict DAF rules are useful bright lines that lower provider costs; the public-support 'conduit' loophole, which lets donors route gifts through DAFs to privately controlled charities, must be closed; endorses the Notice 2017-73 approach, which preserves retail anonymity
comparison_note: §6 and the regulatory tracker do not cover the public-support/Notice 2017-73 issue, which remains open alongside the 4966/6033 guidance project. Leff notes the payout estimates differ mainly by method, as the repo does
independence_note: Author states no external DAF funding

authors: Heist, H. Daniel; Shaker, Genevieve G.; Sumsion, Rachel M.; Tomlinson, Jenna; Minor, Alyssa
title: How Donor Advised Funds Change Fundraising
method: 46 interviews with professional fundraisers; thematic analysis
main_finding: Proposes a 'DAF Donor Relationship Management Cycle' in which gift processing is a critical stage, with reactive and proactive donor identification, six challenges and four opportunities
comparison_note: Agrees with the repo's nonprofit-side findings on DAF grant identification, acknowledgement and data exchange

authors: Shaker, Genevieve G.; Sumsion, Rachel M.; Heist, H. Daniel
title: Reinventing the Cycle: Adapting Relationship Fundraising for Donors Who Use DAFs
retrieval_evidence: PDF downloaded and read (table of contents and front matter); DOI resolves to IU ScholarWorks, 2026-11-15
method: Same fundraiser interview study, practitioner version
main_finding: Six recipient-side challenges: verifying the organisation, investigating DAF donations, entering DAF grants, thanking the donor, understanding DAF rules, exchanging information
comparison_note: The same friction points the repo documents in grant-tracking and payment-rail work

authors: Heist, H. Daniel; Vance-McMullen, Danielle; Sumsion, Rachel; Williams, Jeff (DAF Research Collaborative)
title: The National Survey of Donor Advised Fund Managers
retrieval_evidence: Executive summary PDF downloaded and read; Crossref record + abstract, 2026-11-15
method: Management survey
main_finding: 36% of sponsors send full donor information with grants by default and 24% send the name only; 60% see competition with other sponsors as a barrier; 61% report sufficient IT and 52% sufficient staffing; 35% put great emphasis on keeping every account active; 70% say inactive-account procedures improved donor relations
comparison_note: Sponsor-reported IT gaps (39% not sufficient) and weak relationship functions support the repo's entry-strategy demand thesis (§8). Default donor-information sharing matches the repo's recipient-data findings

authors: Heist, H. Daniel; Vance-McMullen, Danielle; Williams, Jeff; Sumsion, Rachel (DAF Research Collaborative)
title: National Survey of Donor Advised Fund Donors
retrieval_evidence: Executive summary PDF downloaded and read; Crossref record + abstract, 2026-11-15
method: Donor survey
data_and_period: Over 2,100 DAF donors (recruited via participating sponsors)
main_finding: Average age 67; 96% have net worth over $1m; 48% put over 75% of their giving through a DAF in the past three years; giving from other sources is the top reason for lapses in DAF grants (53%); only 9% use an outside financial adviser to manage DAF investments; 72% of anonymous givers want to avoid recognition
comparison_note: The 9% outside-adviser share comes from a sponsor-recruited sample and is not a market share: the repo documents large adviser-managed programs (RCF/Ren channel, MS GIFT, Fidelity CIAP) and 35% of advisers recommending DAFs often (DAFRC 2026). It should not be used to size the channel the 2023 proposed rules would hit
independence_note: Gates Foundation funded; sample recruited through sponsors

authors: Murray, Ian; Heist, Dan; Stone, Kendra
title: Donor Advised Fund Policies and Intergenerational Justice
method: Policy analysis of the Heist-Stone corpus against an intergenerational-justice framework
main_finding: Current inactive-account, endowed-DAF and succession policies partly reflect intergenerational-justice norms, with room for improvement
comparison_note: Normative reading of the same policy data as L14

authors: Vance-McMullen, Danielle; Heist, H. Daniel; Walker Eftin, Lindsey
title: Give Me Some Slack: Donor Advised Fund Granting During Crises
method: Account-level regression of 2020 grantmaking on slack measures
data_and_period: DAFRC account data, 2020 versus prior years
main_finding: Larger accounts, accounts with lower prior payout, frequent contributors and non-endowed accounts gave more in 2020
comparison_note: Low payout partly works as a reserve released in crises. That tempers but does not reverse a 'warehousing' reading of low account medians

title: Unspent Donations in Donor Advised Funds - Policy Recommendation
venue_or_publisher: Hatfield Graduate Journal of Public Affairs 10(1) (published 2026-07-09)
retrieval_evidence: Repository record page with abstract (DOI resolves there), 2026-11-15
method: Policy memo
main_finding: Recommends a federal regulation requiring annual minimum DAF distributions, plus IRS guidance confirming that sponsors may distribute funds on their own authority
comparison_note: Agrees that no payout rule exists. Its regulatory route conflicts with the view, reported in practitioner commentary, that a minimum distribution needs legislation; the 2023 proposed rules adopted none. Low evidentiary weight

authors: Collins, Chuck; DeVaan, Bella; Flannery, Helen (Institute for Policy Studies)
title: The Independent Report on DAFs
method: Form 990 Schedule D/I analysis; IRS payout formula = grants / (year-end assets + grants); sponsor medians; DAF-to-DAF estimate following Giving USA
main_finding: Median sponsor payout is 9.7% in 2023 (9-10% in 2020-23); CFs 9.0%; nationals 14.5-18.0%; donation processors 83.6%; median sponsor-average account size is $135,086 (nationals $390,541; processors $305); DAF-to-DAF grants are at least $4.4bn in 2023 and $10.2bn among nationals in 2020-23; nationals hold 70% of assets
comparison_note: Agrees on direction: CFs pay out the least, processors distort account counts, and DAF-to-DAF flows inflate payout. Levels differ mainly by formula: the repo's median sponsor (>=$1m) is 11-12.5% on beginning assets, while IPS uses year-end assets plus grants and includes small sponsors. The repo's FY2023 central R5 netting of $4.05bn is close to IPS's >=$4.4bn

authors: California Department of Justice, Office of the Attorney General (Registry of Charities and Fundraisers)
title: Donor Advised Funds: An Overview (audit of DAF sponsors registered in California)
venue_or_publisher: California Office of the Attorney General (PDF created 2022-05-18, revised 2022-10-26)
method: Mandatory audit questionnaire covering three reporting periods
data_and_period: 57 sponsors (35 California, 22 national; 29 CF, 11 commercial, 17 mission-based), periods from 2016-07-01 to 2020-12-31
main_finding: $105.3bn of DAF assets at the end of Year 3; about 11% of grants went to other DAFs (CFs 18%, commercial 10%, mission-based 5%); private-foundation contributions were $1.1-1.7bn a year (12% of CF contributions); account grant ratios cluster below 5% and above 50%; administrative fees were $191-267m a year
comparison_note: The 11% DAF-to-DAF share agrees with the repo's 10-18% for nationals. But in California the community foundations, not the nationals, sent the highest share of grants to other DAFs (18%), while the repo frames sponsor-to-sponsor flows as mainly a national-sponsor phenomenon and weights CF recipients by their DAF share. This may partly reflect grants to CF pooled funds

authors: Johnson Center for Philanthropy / Plante Moran for the Council of Michigan Foundations
title: Analysis of Donor Advised Funds from a Community Foundation Perspective
venue_or_publisher: Council of Michigan Foundations / Johnson Center (June 2021)
retrieval_evidence: Landing page fetched 2026-11-15. The full report PDF on michiganfoundations.org is under a robots-disallowed path (/system/files/documents) and was not fetched. Figures are as quoted by IPS 2025 (L28)
method: Account-level DAF records plus Form 990
data_and_period: About 2,600 DAFs at Michigan community foundations, 2017-2020
main_finding: As reported by IPS: median account payout of 3.1% in 2018, against a 5.9% median for Michigan private foundations; more than a quarter of accounts paid nothing in a given year
comparison_note: The lowest account-level CF figure in the literature, versus the repo's CF sponsor median of about 11%. The gap is the sponsor-versus-account distinction. The primary figures are unverified here

title: Impact of the Rise of Commercial Donor-Advised Funds on the Charitable Landscape 1991-2019
venue_or_publisher: Boston College Law School Forum on Philanthropy and the Public Good (May 2021)
retrieval_evidence: BC Law Magazine summary fetched 2026-11-15. The report PDF (ccc.bc.edu/content/dam/...) is robots-disallowed and was not fetched
method: Aggregate giving decomposition (share of individual giving reaching 'working charities')
main_finding: Working charities missed about $300bn in 2014-2018 as giving shifted into DAFs and private foundations
comparison_note: An aggregate, contested estimate that the repo neither tests nor uses. The repo's DAF-to-DAF double-counting findings bear on any total-giving accounting of this kind
independence_note: Authors are reform advocates; methodology publicly disputed (Philanthropy Roundtable brief not retrievable: HTTP 403 challenge)

authors: Han, Xiao; Hungerman, Daniel M.; Ottoni-Wilhelm, Mark
title: Tax Incentives for Charitable Giving: New Findings from the TCJA
method: Panel estimation with a new retiming adjustment
main_finding: The TCJA cut giving by about $20bn a year; moderate retiming after announcement; permanent price elasticity about 0.6 for the average donor and over 2 for the most responsive. The page does not mention DAFs
comparison_note: Context only, not DAF-specific (already in the repo source catalog as C09). No DAF-specific bunching or crowd-out econometrics for 2021-26 was found

venue_or_publisher: DAF Research Collaborative (executive summary PDF created 2026-04-23)

title: Calculating DAF Payout and What We Learn When We Do It Correctly
retrieval_evidence: NBER page HTTP 200, 2026-11-15; already in repo (ANL-27)
method: Payout-methodology critique
main_finding: The industry flow-based payout formula overstates payout by more than 50%; payout must be measured against the asset stock; payout varies widely across sponsors
comparison_note: Dated context (pre-2021). The repo already uses a beginning-assets denominator and nets transfers between sponsors
